newsitem.title: USA: Britain sets review of PacifiCorp's Energy Group bid.
newsitem.headline: Britain sets review of PacifiCorp's Energy Group bid.

text.p: Britain Friday announced an antitrust inquiry into PacifiCorp's planned $6 billion takeover of Energy Group Plc in a sign that the new Labour government may oppose foreign takeovers of British companies.

The move -- the first time a U.S. takeover of a British electric company has been sent for review by antitrust regulators -- sent shares of Energy Group plunging and pushed PacifiCorp stock down as well. PacifiCorp said its bid, worth $9.6 billion including assumption of debt, was on hold pending the review by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.

PacifiCorp said it would cooperate fully with the inquiry. The move by the British government comes after the U.S. Federal Trade Commission also asked for time to consider new information provided by the companies in its antitrust review.
Industry analysts said latest the delay does not mean the deal was off but shows that the government is going to be less tolerant of foreign takeovers.
"They seem to be saying: watch out, the U.K. might not be for sale anymore," said Daniele Seitz, a utility analyst at UBS Securities.
Energy Group owns Eastern Electricity, Britain's largest utility in terms of distribution territory, as well as Peabody Coal Co., the largest coal producer in the United States.
After being privatised in 1990 under the previous Conservative government, all but one of Britain's 12 regional electricity companies have been swallowed by merger partners.

Seven of those deals involved American buyers including Central & Southwest Corp., American Electric Power and Public Service Co. of Colorado. The U.S. utilities cited trans-Atlantic synergies in power supply, technology and generation for the mergers.
Increasing scrunity from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) of utility mergers within the United States has led some companies to look overseas.
After a surge in U.S. mergers about three years ago, lengthy FERC reviews, sometimes lasting two years or more, have stifled the trend, analysts said.

Britain will start to open its retail electricity market to competition in April, while in the United States, California will become the first state to end electric utility monopolies when its market is opened in January.

The Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has been fiercely critical of the previous government's takeover policy and in late June launched a major review of utilities regulation.
The government also vowed to levy a one-time tax on windfall profits of privatised utilities in its first budget.
In mid-June, PacifiCorp announced plans to acquire Energy Group, which was formed in February through the spin-off Hanson Plc's energy assets.
Analysts hailed the deal as a combination of two highly competitive electricity generators that seemed to have common visions for exploiting opportunities in global energy markets.
Analysts said Friday the decision by Margaret Beckett, British Trade and Industry Secretary, to refer the deal to the commission was surprising.
"Obviously there is no possiblity of excess market power -- there is an ocean between the two companies," Sietz at UBS noted.

She and others said British authorities were unlikely to be concerned about the combination of Peabody Coal with PacifiCorp's coal assets since those operations are mostly in the United States and Australia.
"Regulators will do what they want. Depending on what the outcome is, the value of the deal could change," said Linda Byus, an analyst at Nesbitt Burns Securities.
PacifiCorp spokesman Dave Kvamme said the company was disappointed by plans for an investigation, which is scheduled to end in late November.

"Presuming a positive outcome of the Monopolies and Mergers Commission review and approval from Margaret Beckett...we expect to submit another bid (for Energy Group)," Kvamme said, adding the current bid was on hold.
Earlier this week, PacifiCorp said holders representing about two-thirds of Energy Group stock had accepted the offer.
